newsitem.title: UK: Supply one bright spot in euro bond market.
newsitem.headline: Supply one bright spot in euro bond market.

text.p: Growth may be picking up, interest rates may be heading higher, but analysts said one thing the fledgling euro bond market will have in its favour is the driving force in any market -- the balance of supply and demand.
In fact, there was some concern there may not be enough supply to go around if governments and market players do not hurry up and solve some of the technical and legal issues facing the market.
"The supply position will be a plus and will limit the rise in bond yields that one would have otherwise predicted," said Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London.

"Across the whole European Union area deficits are going to be lower in 1999 than they are currently -- not just because of the fiscal retrenchment but more importantly because of cyclical factors with the recovery well under way at that stage," Owens said.
Analysts' projections for growth after planned European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 vary, though many are predicting an upturn in activity.

Price pressures will be building and the new European Central Bank will be keen to establish its inflation-fighting credibility by staying ahead of the curve on interest rates. Interest rate rises may already have come through.
All these factors should weigh on the euro bond market but the swingeing cuts governments have made in public spending to join EMU should be a positive factor.
Analysts said one only needs to look at U.S. Treasuries to see how quickly the supply picture can improve the outlook for the market.
U.S. government debt has been bolstered recently by news that the Treasury has scrapped sales of conventional 10-year notes in July and October because of progress in cutting the budget deficit.

But Mark Fox, chief European strategist for fixed income at Lehman Brothers in London, said while the supply picture may be positive at the federal level it may not be for those issuers further down the ladder.

"What you will see is a significant increase in the amount of debt issuance on the part of municipalities, local authorities, provinces, cities and so on," he said. "(EMU) will be marginally good for supply but more than anything else what you will see is a change in the nature of supply," he said.
Analysts added technical and legal issues still need to be tackled to ensure deep and liquid supply. Governments and market players must decide whether to redenominate or renominalise debt.

Redenominating means converting the debt into euros at a currency's conversion rate but that leaves the market to cope with odd numbers. Renominalising means rounding the amounts and then compensating for any differentials.

A third issue is reconventioning. Will rules governing such issues as day count and coupon payment methods be different for euro bonds? A harmonised system would seem logical but how will the old and new debt mesh?

So far, only France, Belgium and Luxembourg, have said they will redenominate their outstanding debt into euros from the outset in 1999. Juergen Stark, state secretary in the German finance ministry has said he would recommend that all tradable federal government debt be converted into the euro from 1999 but a final decision has not yet been made.

"If it were only new issues in tradable debt the debt market will have a rough time getting off the ground and you would immediately have problems between the cash and derivatives markets," said Daniel Gros, senior research fellow at the Centre for European Studies in Brussels.
"That's the key issue and even in Bonn why they're thinking of redenominating their debt in euro."
Redenomination is easier for countries like France where much of the debt information is "dematerialised" or held on computer, analysts said.
"In France most public debt does not exist on paper," Gros said. "In Germany it does, and that makes it very difficult," he said.
Analysts said all these issues may affect bondholders' rights and bondholders meetings may have to be held to approve any changes.

"You get false comfort if you assume that, without harmonising market conventions, by changing the currency of payment and even the way you package it that you have enhanced liquidity," said Jeffrey Golden, a partner at legal firm Allen & Overy in London, which is European counsel for the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA).
Analysts said with the 1999 start date fast approaching, these issues need to be worked out soon.
"The problem is you cannot just say I redenominate and push a button and that's it," Gros said.
